# Wisdom of Solomon Chapter 4 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Vaticanus, Wisdom 4 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/WIS_004_page_001.jpg

---

**4:1** A life of virtue without children is better than a large family without virtue. Virtue carries its own immortality — in the memory it leaves behind, in the recognition it receives from both God and human beings.

**4:2** While virtue is present, people imitate it. When it is gone, they ache for it. All through time, virtue moves crowned and victorious — winning in every undefiled contest.

**4:3** The ungodly may produce many children, but that abundance is worthless. Their illegitimate branches will find no deep soil, no firm footing.

**4:4** Let them put out growth for a season — wind is enough to shake them, and when it strengthens, they will be torn up entirely. They have no roots.

**4:5** Their branches will snap before they ripen. Their fruit will be useless — inedible, fit for nothing.

**4:6** Children born of unlawful unions become evidence against their parents when the time of accounting arrives.

**4:7** But the righteous person — even one who dies young — has already found rest.

**4:8** Old age is not something earned by accumulating years. You do not honor it simply by living a long time.

**4:9** The true grey hair of a human life is understanding. A blameless life is what real old age looks like.

**4:10** Once there was a man who pleased God and was deeply loved by him. While surrounded by sinners, he was taken away.

**4:11** He was snatched away before wickedness could warp his judgment, before deception could corrupt his soul.

**4:12** The spell that trivial things cast over us obscures what is truly good. Desire, when it wanders, hollows out even an innocent mind.

**4:13** He was perfected in a short time and fulfilled the measure of many years.

**4:14** His soul was pleasing to the Lord — and so the Lord, out of love, quickly removed him from the midst of wickedness.

**4:15** People see all this and still don't grasp it. They don't take it in: that God's grace and mercy rest on his chosen, that he watches over those who belong to him.

**4:16** The righteous person who died will stand as judge over those ungodly ones who are still alive. A life completed early will expose the emptiness of the ungodly's long old age.

**4:17** They will witness the wise person's end and not understand what God was doing — why he kept him safe, what he had planned for him.

**4:18** They will sneer at him — and God will sneer back at them.

**4:19** After that, they will become a dishonored corpse, a scandal among the dead for all time. God will shatter them into silence, tear them up from their foundations, leave them utterly ruined and in agony. Their very memory will be erased.

**4:20** They will come, filled with terror, to face the account of their sins. Everything they did in defiance of God will be brought before them, right to their face.

---

*PNEUMA notes: The Enoch allusion (v. 10) is handled by setting the scene — "Once there was a man" — which makes the paradigm accessible without requiring footnotes. The "spell" language of v. 12 (goēteia) is rendered as "spell" to retain the disturbing sorcery image. The chapter's central argument — that early death can be completion, not failure — is emphasized through the phrasing at vv. 13-14.*
